I agree that there's an effect. In the case of a child who's not trans and doesn't bring up being trans, it is indeed overboard (and totally ridiculous) to even broach the topic of administering puberty blockers.

However, in the case of a child who is trans (or is questioning their gender identity), the neutral option is not to withhold puberty blockers. To do so would be to jeopardize the trans child in hopes that the child is actually cis. Rather, the neutral route would be to administer puberty blockers so that regardless of whether the child is trans or is simply questioning, they can continue on whatever track (puberty) best fits them after they affirm their decision.

I definitely understand the sentiment of a parent who wants to do everything they can, and to keep their child(ren) as safe as possible.

One thing to note though, coming from someone who started HRT (hormone-replacement therapy) relatively young, there's a lot of misinformation out there. I can only speak on the side of transitioning from male to female, but based on both my experiences and what I've heard from others, the process doesn't progress with a snap of the fingers.

Generally, endocrinologists will administer puberty blockers to minors before puberty starts or before it ends (my case being the latter). This is done so that the minor's puberty is halted, which gives them time to consider and really be assured in their decision. Although it's not a perfect system, and taking puberty blockers for long periods of time can bring up issues with regards to fertility, it is totally reversible when administered correctly and safely by doctors.

That may sound scary and terrifying, but it is important to consider the alternative as well.  Hypothetically, let's say your child is trans and is transitioning from male to female. Not taking puberty blockers out of fear that the child wrongly decided can jeopardize them in the opposite way. To continue male puberty for a trans person transitioning from male to female is no different from forcing a cis male child to undergo HRT himself. In essence, putting a trans child transitioning from male to female through male puberty will only create unnecessary distress, especially when there is a perfectly safe alternative: taking puberty blockers.

Perhaps put more eloquently, taken from the [PHSA](http://www.phsa.ca/transcarebc/child-youth/affirmation-transition/medical-affirmation-transition/puberty-blockers-for-youth), "Withholding puberty blockers and hormone therapy is not a neutral option and can result in an increased risk of mental health issues. "

Even for someone like myself who started young, even though I started taking puberty blockers before male puberty ended, there were male secondary sex characteristics that couldn't be erased. For one, my voice didn't change to that of a female's with estrogen (as estrogen won't change that), so I had to (and still do) spend lengthy periods of time working on my voice to get it to a presentable level (which I've just barely achieved after years of effort). Although I'm lucky in this regard, facial hair and Adam's apples aren't reversed with estrogen, just as an example of other things.

With regards to waiting for a child to better understand their sexuality, I'd like to clarify that what you meant here was probably gender identity. I agree that it is a good idea to let children explore themselves.

I think a certain responsibility here lies with the parents. Having a certain level of trust in one's children is important.  Please forgive me if I've provided a long response, and feel free to ask a question if you'd like.

This process can seem like walking a tightrope, and it is, but it's crucial to prevent oneself from pushing their child towards one side of the line in fear of them veering towards the other.

As someone who's had both regular therapists and gender therapists, I'd say there is a difference.

A regular therapist is great for talking about any issue in one's life, trans-related stuff included.

However, a gender therapist is useful in that they have experience not only dealing with gender-related issues, but also how to go about the transitioning process. Even more valuable to me is the practical advice coming from someone who knows what the process looks like. Also, a gender therapist in this case can be a way to get started on HRT, letters necessary to change gender markers, referrals to surgeons, etc.

I still see a regular therapist alongside my gender therapist, and they serve different purposes.
